title: Break the work into epics and a backlog
summary: Turn the first release into a backlog the team can work from: a few large epics, each broken into smaller items, in priority order. A good backlog makes progress visible and planning easy.

beginner: Take each part of the first release and make it an epic, a large piece of work with a clear goal.
Break each epic into smaller items that deliver something a user or the team can see.
Write a short title and a sentence of context for each item. Detail comes later.
Put the items in priority order, with the riskiest and most valuable near the top.
Mark dependencies between items and on other teams.
Review the backlog with the team and agree who keeps it tidy.
intermediate: Create epics for each part of the release, each with a goal and measure.
Split epics into small, valuable items and order them by value and risk.
Mark dependencies and link items to the product brief.
Agree backlog ownership and a refinement rhythm.
experienced: Structure the backlog around outcomes, so every item traces to a goal.
Keep only the next few weeks detailed; leave later work at epic level.
Expose cross-team dependencies early and agree them with the other teams.
Regularly prune items that no longer serve the goal.

canDelegateTo.task: Create and order the backlog items
Break epics into items and capture details

toolExamples.jira: Create epics, link stories to them and use the backlog view to drag items into order.
toolExamples.azure-devops: Use features and user stories under epics, and order them on the backlog board.
toolExamples.linear: Use projects for epics and keep the issue list ordered by priority.
toolExamples.trello: Use one list per epic and order cards from top to bottom by priority.
toolExamples.claude: Paste the product brief and ask it to suggest epics and a first breakdown, then refine it with the team.

definitionOfDone: Epics created for the first release, each with a goal
Epics broken into smaller items and ordered by priority
Dependencies marked and backlog owner agreed
pitfalls: Writing detailed items for work months away
Splitting work by technical layer instead of user value
A backlog so long nobody can see the priorities

sources.title: Making sense of MVP (Henrik Kniberg, Crisp)
